questions.explanationHtml: Single-case studies (n = 1) cannot establish population norms. Gardner's self-report of full recovery has been contradicted by his later accounts of long-term insomnia. Controlled chronic sleep-restriction studies show cumulative cognitive, metabolic and affective deficits. Krause et al. (2017) demonstrated that even one night of total sleep deprivation amplifies amygdala reactivity to negative stimuli by ~60% with reduced prefrontal regulatory connectivity — a plausible neural substrate for the well-documented sleep–mood link.

subChunks.title: Stress Physiology & Neuroplasticity
subChunks.hookHtml: In the year 2000, Eleanor Maguire scanned the brains of sixteen London taxi drivers and showed that their posterior hippocampi were measurably larger than those of matched controls — and grew larger still the longer they had been driving. The brain, it turned out, was not the fixed organ Cajal had described a century earlier ('In the adult centres the nerve paths are something fixed, ended, immutable. Everything may die, nothing may be regenerated'). It was a dynamic, plastic system, reshaping itself in response to experience throughout life. At roughly the same time, Bruce McEwen was demonstrating the dark mirror image of this plasticity: chronic stress, sustained over years, was eating away at the very same hippocampus. The story of stress physiology and neuroplasticity is the story of how experience writes itself into the architecture of the brain — for better and for worse.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Selye and the General Adaptation Syndrome

Hans Selye (1956) The Stress of Life formalised the concept of stress as a non-specific physiological response to demand. His General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) proposed three stages:

  1. Alarm reaction: immediate sympathomedullary activation — adrenaline and noradrenaline are released from the adrenal medulla, producing the classical fight-or-flight response (increased heart rate, raised blood pressure, pupil dilation, glucose mobilisation).
  2. Resistance: if the stressor persists, the body attempts to adapt. The HPA axis sustains elevated cortisol, parasympathetic recovery is partial, and outwardly the individual may appear to cope. Internally, immune function and reproductive systems are suppressed.
  3. Exhaustion: prolonged demand depletes physiological reserves. Susceptibility to illness rises sharply; Selye called the diseases of this phase 'diseases of adaptation' — including hypertension, ulcers, and immunosuppression.

Evaluation: Selye's model was foundational but criticised on several grounds. (i) The 'non-specificity' claim was always overstated — stressors produce partly differentiated physiological signatures (Mason, 1971). (ii) The model is largely physiological and underplays cognitive appraisal — Lazarus & Folkman's (1984) transactional model offered a more psychologically rich account in which stress is the product of primary (threat) and secondary (coping) appraisals. (iii) Most empirical work was conducted on rats; human stress involves social, symbolic and anticipatory dimensions absent in laboratory rodents.

The HPA Axis in Depth

The hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis is the slow arm of the stress response.

  1. The paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus releases corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH) into the hypophyseal portal system.
  2. CRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) into the systemic circulation.
  3. ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata) to synthesise and release cortisol.
  4. Cortisol exerts diverse effects: mobilises glucose, suppresses inflammation acutely, suppresses immune and reproductive function chronically, and crosses the blood–brain barrier to bind glucocorticoid receptors throughout the cortex and limbic system.
  5. Cortisol exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, normally shutting down its own release once homeostasis is restored.

Chronic stress disrupts this feedback. Hippocampal neurons are unusually dense in glucocorticoid receptors; under chronic cortisol exposure, they undergo dendritic atrophy and, in extreme cases, cell death (Sapolsky, 1996). Because the hippocampus normally helps inhibit HPA activity, its atrophy disinhibits the axis — a self-amplifying cycle.

Sympathomedullary Pathway

The faster arm of the stress response is the sympathetic–adrenal medullary (SAM) pathway. Hypothalamic signals descend via sympathetic chain ganglia to the adrenal medulla, which secretes adrenaline (epinephrine, ~80%) and noradrenaline (~20%) directly into the bloodstream. These catecholamines mediate the acute fight-or-flight response — onset within seconds, peak within minutes, dissipation within tens of minutes. The SAM pathway is calibrated for short, intense bursts of demand; the HPA axis is calibrated for sustained challenge.

Allostatic Load: McEwen's Reframing

Bruce McEwen (1998) New England Journal of Medicine, and in subsequent reviews (McEwen, 2002), introduced the concept of allostasis — the active process of maintaining stability through change — and allostatic load, the cumulative physiological cost of chronic adaptive demand. Allostatic load can arise from: (i) frequent stressors; (ii) failure to habituate to repeated stressors; (iii) inability to terminate the stress response promptly; or (iv) inadequate response (necessitating compensatory elevations elsewhere).

Indices of allostatic load include elevated resting cortisol and catecholamines, hypertension, central adiposity, dyslipidaemia, glycated haemoglobin, and reduced heart-rate variability. McEwen's framework links the molecular biology of glucocorticoids to the epidemiology of socio-economic health disparities: chronic adversity produces chronic allostatic load, which produces excess morbidity and mortality.

Stress, Immunity & the Common Cold

Sheldon Cohen and colleagues (1991) New England Journal of Medicine conducted the classic empirical demonstration of stress–immune coupling in humans. 394 healthy adults completed psychological stress measures and were then nasally inoculated with one of five respiratory viruses (with informed consent and medical oversight). The rate of clinical colds rose monotonically with stress index — from approximately 27% in low-stress participants to nearly 47% in high-stress participants. The relationship survived adjustment for age, sex, weight, antibody status, and health behaviours. More recent work (Cohen et al., 2012) demonstrates that chronic stress downregulates glucocorticoid receptor sensitivity in immune cells, releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines from normal cortisol-mediated restraint — a mechanism linking stress to chronic inflammatory and cardiovascular disease.

Neuroplasticity: The Brain Rewrites Itself

For most of the twentieth century, the adult brain was believed to be structurally fixed. Modern neuroscience has comprehensively overturned this view.

Maguire et al. (2000): London Taxi Drivers

Eleanor Maguire and colleagues (2000) PNAS used voxel-based morphometry to compare 16 male London taxi drivers — required to pass 'The Knowledge', an exhaustive examination of London's 25,000 streets — with matched controls. Posterior hippocampal volume was significantly greater in taxi drivers, and volume correlated positively with years of driving experience. Anterior hippocampal volume showed the opposite pattern — suggesting reallocation, not simply growth. A subsequent longitudinal study (Woollett & Maguire, 2011) tracked trainees over four years, showing that posterior hippocampal increases emerged specifically in those who qualified, not in those who failed — strengthening the causal interpretation.

Draganski et al. (2004): Juggling

Draganski et al. (2004) Nature randomly assigned non-jugglers to a juggling-training group or a control group. After three months of training, jugglers showed grey-matter expansion in mid-temporal area and posterior intraparietal sulcus — regions involved in visual motion processing. Three months after ceasing training, the gains had partly receded. This was the first prospective randomised demonstration in humans that grey-matter structure changes with skill acquisition over weeks.

Critical and Sensitive Periods

A critical period is a developmental window during which a particular experience is required for normal development; if missed, the relevant function cannot be acquired (Hubel & Wiesel's monocular-deprivation work in kittens established the principle for ocular dominance columns). A sensitive period is a softer concept: a window during which experience has heightened effect but learning remains possible afterwards. Language acquisition shows sensitive-period properties — the dramatic case of Genie (Curtiss, 1977), who was deprived of linguistic input until age 13, illustrates the cost of late exposure but also the partial — if limited — capacity for later acquisition.

Recovery from Brain Damage

Damaged brains can recover function through several mechanisms:

  • Functional reorganisation: intact regions take over functions of damaged ones. Phineas Gage's gradual partial recovery and patient H.M.'s preserved procedural learning illustrate the brain's capacity to redistribute function within constraints.
  • Axonal sprouting and synaptic reorganisation: surviving neurons grow new connections to replace lost inputs.
  • Neurogenesis: long denied in the adult mammalian brain, neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus was demonstrated definitively in humans by Eriksson et al. (1998) Nature Medicine using BrdU labelling in cancer patients. More recent work (Boldrini et al., 2018) has confirmed adult hippocampal neurogenesis across the lifespan, though the field remains contested following Sorrells et al. (2018) reporting reduced neurogenesis in adults.
  • Constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT): developed by Taub (Taub et al., 1993) for stroke rehabilitation, CIMT restrains the unaffected limb, forcing intensive use of the affected limb. Randomised trials (Wolf et al., 2006 EXCITE trial) demonstrate sustained improvements in motor function, with corresponding cortical reorganisation visible on neuroimaging.

Recent Developments

Snyder et al. (2022) Nature demonstrated that chronic psychosocial stress in mice produces persistent epigenetic remodelling of hippocampal neurons, with corresponding behavioural anhedonia — strengthening the molecular bridge from stress to depression. In humans, Park et al. (2021) showed that chronic stress measured by hair cortisol predicts later hippocampal volume loss prospectively, supporting causal direction. Neuroplasticity research is now integrating with epigenetics, immunology, and the gut microbiome — fields once unimaginable to Selye but consistent with the principle he intuited: the body is one integrated adaptive system.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: For most of the twentieth century we believed the adult brain was fixed. Cajal himself wrote that nothing in the central nervous system could be regenerated. Maguire's taxi-driver study in 2000 was one of several findings that overturned that orthodoxy. Learning twenty-five thousand London streets visibly enlarged the posterior hippocampus. Experience reshapes neuroanatomy.

storyBeats.speaker: Selye's GAS in Selye's own life
storyBeats.text: Hans Selye coined the modern psychological use of the word 'stress' in the 1930s after watching laboratory rats develop ulcers, immune suppression and adrenal enlargement regardless of which stressor he used — cold, surgery, or restraint. His General Adaptation Syndrome — alarm, resistance, exhaustion — became the foundation of modern stress physiology, even as later researchers refined and challenged his claim that the response was wholly non-specific.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Selye gave us the architecture: two pathways. The fast sympathomedullary pathway floods the body with adrenaline within seconds. The slower HPA axis releases cortisol over minutes, hours, and days. Acutely, both are adaptive. Chronically, they become corrosive. Bruce McEwen called this 'allostatic load' — the accumulating cost of being adaptive for too long.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Sheldon Cohen showed how concrete the cost can be. He measured psychological stress in nearly four hundred volunteers, then exposed them to common-cold viruses under controlled conditions. The most stressed group caught colds at almost twice the rate of the least stressed. Subjective stress, measured weeks earlier, predicted immune failure in a laboratory infection.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: And then there is the brighter side. Draganski's juggling study in Nature randomly assigned non-jugglers to learn. Three months later, grey matter in visual-motion areas had measurably expanded. Stop juggling and it partly receded. Eriksson's 1998 Nature Medicine paper proved that adult humans grow new neurons in the dentate gyrus. The plasticity that experience exploits is the same plasticity that stress endangers — and the same plasticity that recovery, with the right scaffolding, can mobilise.

A student asks how this changes clinical practice. Dr. Chen answers without hesitation: 'It means we should stop telling patients their brains are fixed. Constraint-induced movement therapy, cognitive rehabilitation, intensive practice — these work because plasticity is a permanent feature of the central nervous system, not a privilege of childhood.'

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Scenario: Dr. Lin, a junior doctor, has worked twelve-hour night shifts in A&E for the past eighteen months. She presents to her own GP reporting persistent fatigue, increasing frequency of upper respiratory infections, weight gain around the waist, mild hypertension, and a recent depressive episode.

Using your knowledge of stress physiology, explain Dr. Lin's symptom cluster. In your response, address: (1) how chronic activation of the HPA axis produces sustained cortisol elevation and what its downstream effects are; (2) why elevated cortisol predisposes to infection (citing Cohen et al., 1991); (3) how McEwen's concept of allostatic load helps integrate the cluster into a single framework. Aim for 100–130 words.

Guidance: Begin with one sentence linking chronic HPA activation to cortisol. Then walk through three downstream consequences (immune suppression, central adiposity, hippocampal effects on mood). Cite Cohen and McEwen by name. Close with a sentence on why this is a systems-level problem requiring more than symptomatic treatment.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Dr. Lin's symptoms reflect chronic activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, resulting in sustained elevation of cortisol. While adaptive in acute crises, chronic cortisol exposure produces severe downstream consequences: it suppresses immune function, promotes central adiposity (waist weight gain), and can cause hippocampal dendritic atrophy, increasing vulnerability to depression.

The link to her frequent respiratory infections is well-established; Cohen et al. (1991) demonstrated that chronic psychological stress directly predicts susceptibility to clinical colds following viral exposure, as cortisol-mediated restraint on inflammation fails. McEwen's concept of 'allostatic load' integrates her fatigue, hypertension, weight gain, and depression into a single framework — they represent the cumulative physiological wear-and-tear of adapting to relentless demand. Treating these symptoms individually would fail to address the underlying systems-level exhaustion driving her presentation.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A neurologist tells the family of a stroke patient: 'I'm sorry — at her age, the brain cannot recover. What is lost is lost.' Drawing on your understanding of neuroplasticity (Maguire et al., 2000; Draganski et al., 2004), adult neurogenesis (Eriksson et al., 1998), and constraint-induced movement therapy (Taub et al., 1993; Wolf et al., 2006), critically evaluate this claim. Discuss what the evidence does and does not support, and what an evidence-based prognosis would look like. Aim for 130+ words and write in academic register with named citations.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a stressed-out friend why 'just being stressed for a few months' can show up as a real, physical change in the brain and body, not just in their mood.
subChunks.modelAnswer: The neurologist's framing reflects a twentieth-century orthodoxy that contemporary neuroscience has substantially revised. While there are real limits to recovery — particularly in older patients with extensive lesions involving white-matter tracts — the assertion that 'the brain cannot recover' is empirically untenable. First, structural neuroplasticity persists into adulthood. Maguire et al.'s (2000) PNAS study demonstrated experience-dependent posterior hippocampal expansion in adult London taxi drivers, with volume correlating with years of experience; Woollett & Maguire's (2011) longitudinal follow-up showed the expansion emerged specifically in those who qualified for licensure, supporting a causal interpretation. Draganski et al.'s (2004) Nature study randomised adult non-jugglers to training, showing grey-matter expansion in visual-motion areas after three months. Plasticity is therefore not confined to development. Second, adult neurogenesis has been demonstrated in humans. Eriksson et al.'s (1998) Nature Medicine paper used BrdU labelling in cancer patients to show new neurons in the adult dentate gyrus; Boldrini et al. (2018) confirmed lifelong hippocampal neurogenesis, although Sorrells et al. (2018) report reduced rates — the field remains active. Neurogenesis is one of several mechanisms (alongside axonal sprouting and functional reorganisation) by which damaged brains repair partially. Third, targeted rehabilitation can mobilise plasticity for clinical benefit. Constraint-induced movement therapy (Taub et al., 1993; Wolf et al.'s 2006 EXCITE randomised trial) restrains the unaffected limb to force intensive use of the affected one, producing sustained motor improvements and visible cortical reorganisation even years post-stroke. An evidence-based prognosis would communicate that recovery is partial, time-consuming and effortful — but not impossible — and that intensive, structured rehabilitation can meaningfully improve outcome. Therapeutic nihilism is not warranted by current evidence and may itself worsen prognosis by reducing engagement.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Selye's (1956) three-stage model of the stress response: alarm (acute sympathetic activation), resistance (sustained HPA-mediated adaptation), and exhaustion (depletion and disease). Foundational but criticised for understating cognitive appraisal and stressor specificity.

The hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis: CRH from the hypothalamus stimulates pituitary ACTH, which stimulates adrenal cortisol release. Chronic activation disrupts negative feedback and is implicated in hippocampal atrophy, depression and immune dysregulation.

McEwen's (1998, 2002) concept of the cumulative physiological cost of chronic adaptive demand, indexed by elevated baseline cortisol, blood pressure, central adiposity, dyslipidaemia, and inflammatory markers.

The generation of new neurons. Demonstrated in the adult human dentate gyrus by Eriksson et al. (1998) via BrdU labelling; subsequent work (Boldrini et al., 2018; Sorrells et al., 2018) has both extended and challenged the finding.

A developmental window during which a particular experience is necessary for normal development of a function. Established by Hubel & Wiesel's monocular deprivation studies in kittens; contrasted with the softer 'sensitive period'.

A rehabilitation technique (Taub et al., 1993) restraining the unaffected limb to force use of the affected limb after stroke or brain injury, producing sustained motor recovery and visible cortical reorganisation (Wolf et al., 2006).

questions.questionHtml: Which sequence correctly describes the cascade of the HPA axis from initial signal to systemic effect?
options: ACTH (hypothalamus) → CRH (pituitary) → adrenaline (adrenal medulla)
CRH (hypothalamus) → ACTH (pituitary) → cortisol (adrenal cortex)
Cortisol (hypothalamus) → CRH (pituitary) → ACTH (adrenal medulla)
Adrenaline (hypothalamus) → cortisol (pituitary) → ACTH (adrenal cortex)
questions.explanationHtml: The HPA cascade begins with corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH) from the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH), which in turn stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol. Cortisol then exerts negative feedback on hypothalamus and pituitary — a feedback loop disrupted under chronic stress.

questions.questionHtml: Eriksson et al.'s (1998) study using BrdU labelling demonstrated that adult humans generate new neurons in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus.
questions.explanationHtml: Eriksson and colleagues used BrdU — a thymidine analogue incorporated into DNA during cell division — that had been administered to terminal cancer patients for diagnostic purposes. Post-mortem analysis revealed BrdU-labelled neurons in the adult human dentate gyrus, providing the first definitive demonstration of adult hippocampal neurogenesis. Later work (Boldrini et al., 2018; Sorrells et al., 2018) has extended and contested the magnitude of the phenomenon, but the basic finding overturned the longstanding 'no new neurons' orthodoxy.

questions.questionHtml: A 55-year-old stroke patient is left with reduced use of her right arm. Her physiotherapist proposes constraint-induced movement therapy. Which rationale best explains the expected mechanism of benefit?
options: The unaffected limb is restrained to prevent overuse injury
Restraining the unaffected limb forces intensive use of the affected limb, driving cortical reorganisation and functional recovery
CIMT works only via pharmacological augmentation; the restraint is incidental
CIMT prevents neurogenesis to stabilise existing connections
questions.correctAnswer: Restraining the unaffected limb forces intensive use of the affected limb, driving cortical reorganisation and functional recovery
questions.explanationHtml: CIMT (Taub et al., 1993) was developed on the principle of overcoming 'learned non-use' — patients spontaneously favour the unaffected limb, and the affected limb's cortical representation shrinks further. Forced intensive use drives experience-dependent cortical reorganisation; the Wolf et al. (2006) EXCITE randomised trial demonstrated sustained motor improvement with corresponding neuroimaging changes.

questions.questionHtml: Cohen et al. (1991) found that psychological stress predicted clinical cold rates after viral inoculation. A student concludes: 'Therefore, stress causes colds directly, independent of any other factor.' Which evaluation is most accurate?
options: Cohen's design was prospective with viral inoculation and statistical control for confounders, supporting a causal role for stress operating partly via glucocorticoid-mediated immune dysregulation (Cohen et al., 2012) — though stress is one contributory factor among many, not the sole cause
The study was purely correlational with no statistical control and supports no causal inference
Cohen's design proves stress is the single sufficient cause of all common colds
The study's findings have been entirely overturned by recent research
questions.correctAnswer: Cohen's design was prospective with viral inoculation and statistical control for confounders, supporting a causal role for stress operating partly via glucocorticoid-mediated immune dysregulation (Cohen et al., 2012) — though stress is one contributory factor among many, not the sole cause
questions.explanationHtml: Cohen's (1991) design was unusually strong: psychological measures were taken before controlled viral exposure, with statistical adjustment for age, sex, weight, antibody status, and health behaviours. The dose–response relationship across stress quintiles supports a causal interpretation. Later mechanistic work (Cohen et al., 2012) implicates downregulated glucocorticoid-receptor sensitivity in immune cells, releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines from cortisol-mediated restraint. Stress is contributory, not sufficient; the student's framing overstates the inference.
